candidates.questionText: A patient asks why the dentist might request images after examining the mouth. What additional information can radiographs provide?

answers.text: Conditions hidden from direct clinical inspection
A replacement for the medical history
A definitive diagnosis of every oral lesion
Proof that future dental disease cannot develop

candidates.explanation: Radiographs can reveal otherwise unseen disease. They supplement history and examination; they neither diagnose every lesion nor predict freedom from future disease.

candidates.questionText: According to the ADA’s 2026 summary, which imaging approach is primary for an initial endodontic evaluation?

answers.text: Routine CBCT before clinical examination
Intraoral two-dimensional radiographs
Panoramic imaging as the only assessment
CBCT instead of all intraoral imaging

candidates.explanation: Intraoral 2D imaging is the primary initial modality. CBCT may follow clinical and 2D assessment when indicated; neither automatic CBCT nor panoramic imaging alone is the stated primary approach.

candidates.questionText: What distinguishes the image data produced by dental CBCT from a conventional two-dimensional dental radiograph?

answers.text: A single flat projection
A set of external facial photographs
A three-dimensional reconstruction
A continuous two-dimensional display

candidates.explanation: CBCT reconstructs a volume from X-ray projections. A single flat projection, external photographs, or a continuous 2D display does not describe that volumetric result.

candidates.questionText: Before a panoramic exposure, earrings lie within the imaging region. What should the team do to reduce interference?

answers.text: Increase exposure time
Correct all interference afterward
Leave them in place if the patient is still
Ask the patient to remove them

candidates.explanation: Metal in the imaging region can interfere with the image. Removal addresses this risk; extra exposure, stillness alone, or assumed software correction does not remove the object.

candidates.questionText: What is the purpose of correct bite-block and head positioning during panoramic acquisition?

answers.text: Align the teeth and head for a clear image
Replace the need to keep still
Determine whether imaging is clinically indicated
Set the exposure automatically for every patient

candidates.explanation: Positioning supports image clarity and alignment. It does not replace stillness, establish clinical need, or determine a universal exposure setting.

candidates.questionText: During a dental CBCT acquisition, what instruction should the patient follow as the source and detector move?

answers.text: Turn the head to follow the detector
Remain still in the position established by the team
Reposition the chin at each projection
Open and close the mouth throughout the scan

candidates.explanation: The team positions the patient before acquisition; the patient then remains still. Following the detector, moving the chin, or repeatedly moving the jaw conflicts with that instruction.

candidates.questionText: An operator repeatedly raises digital exposure to make image noise less noticeable. Which concern does this illustrate?

answers.text: A reduction in patient exposure
Removal of the need for quality control
Exposure creep
A substitute for patient positioning

candidates.explanation: Exposure creep describes dose increases made to suppress visible noise. It increases rather than reduces exposure and does not replace quality control or positioning.

candidates.questionText: When selecting exposure for a justified dental image, which quality goal fits optimization?

answers.text: The smoothest image regardless of dose
The lowest setting even if anatomy is unreadable
The same setting for every patient
Diagnostic adequacy at the lowest reasonably needed dose

candidates.explanation: Optimization balances usable diagnostic information with dose reduction. Cosmetic smoothness, unreadable minimum-dose images, and universal settings fail that balance.

candidates.questionText: A patient is worried about a recommended CBCT examination. What is the most appropriate response before proceeding?

answers.text: Invite discussion with the dentist about its purpose, benefits, risks and alternatives
Promise that the examination has no radiation risk
State that owning a scanner makes the examination necessary
Explain that questions should wait until after exposure

candidates.explanation: FDA encourages informed discussion before imaging. Zero-risk assurances are inaccurate; equipment availability is not justification, and postponing questions prevents that discussion.

candidates.questionText: For periodontal evaluation, which approach does the ADA’s 2026 summary identify as the established standard?

answers.text: Routine CBCT without clinical examination
A 2D full-mouth series together with clinical examination
A panoramic image without clinical findings
Imaging only after all treatment is finished

candidates.explanation: The summary supports a full-mouth 2D series plus examination. Routine CBCT, an isolated panoramic image, or deferring all imaging until after treatment does not describe that approach.

candidates.questionText: As an X-ray beam passes through a patient, what happens to its photons?

answers.text: All are stored in the tissues
All reach the detector unchanged
Some are absorbed or scattered, while others are transmitted
All are converted into visible light before reaching the detector

candidates.explanation: The detector receives the transmitted pattern after absorption and scattering within the patient. Storage, unchanged transmission of every photon, and complete conversion to visible light are not this process.

candidates.questionText: Why does ionizing radiation used in dental imaging require protection measures?

answers.text: It makes every exposed patient develop cancer
Its effects are limited to warming the skin
It cannot interact with living cells
It can damage DNA

candidates.explanation: Ionizing radiation can damage DNA and increase cancer risk. Risk is not a certainty of cancer; neither heat alone nor an inability to interact with cells describes the concern.

candidates.questionText: Why is particular attention to radiation protection appropriate for children?

answers.text: They are more radiosensitive and have more remaining years for effects to develop
They receive no natural background radiation
They cannot benefit from diagnostically necessary images
They have the same risk per unit dose as every adult

candidates.explanation: FDA identifies greater radiosensitivity and a longer remaining lifetime. Background exposure is not absent, necessary imaging can benefit children, and equal risk per unit dose is not the stated basis.

candidates.questionText: A small child needs a justified X-ray examination. How should exposure settings be selected?

answers.text: Use adult settings because the equipment is the same
Use an appropriate pediatric protocol considering size and the clinical task
Use age alone and disregard body size
Use the maximum setting to avoid any chance of noise

candidates.explanation: FDA emphasizes patient size, the clinical task and pediatric protocols. Adult defaults, age alone, or maximum exposure can give inappropriate dose; adequate image quality remains necessary.

candidates.questionText: The dentist determines that a lower-exposure examination can supply all information needed for a clinical question. What supports radiation protection?

answers.text: Add CBCT solely because it produces 3D images
Acquire both examinations routinely
Use the adequate lower-exposure option
Use CBCT whenever the scanner is available

candidates.explanation: CBCT should be justified by information not adequately supplied by lower-exposure options. Routine duplication, 3D capability alone, and availability do not establish that need.

candidates.questionText: Which change directly restricts the X-ray beam to the region that needs imaging?

answers.text: Increase display brightness
Lengthen the exposure
Enlarge the irradiated field
Use rectangular collimation

candidates.explanation: Rectangular collimation limits the beam’s extent. Display brightness changes viewing, while longer exposure or a larger field does not restrict the irradiated region.

candidates.questionText: What do the ADA’s 2024 recommendations advise about routine patient lead aprons and thyroid collars for dental imaging?

answers.text: Discontinue routine use while following applicable regulations
Require them for every patient regardless of regulations
Use them instead of limiting beam size
Use them to justify otherwise unnecessary imaging

candidates.explanation: ADA advises against routine patient shielding and notes possible beam obstruction. Applicable rules still matter. Shielding neither replaces beam limitation nor justifies imaging; universal mandatory use is not the ADA recommendation.

candidates.questionText: A new patient reports recent images from another dental office. What step may avoid unnecessary repeat exposure?

answers.text: Repeat the entire series before requesting records
Request the existing images for the dentist to assess
Assume outside images are unusable
Treat a change of office as an automatic indication for new images

candidates.explanation: Existing images may meet the dentist’s information needs. Their adequacy should be assessed; relocation, assumed unusability, or repeating before review does not establish a need for new exposure.

candidates.questionText: After removing a used barrier from an X-ray control surface, the assistant sees contamination underneath. What is required before the next patient?

answers.text: Place a new barrier over the contamination
Wipe with a dry towel only
Clean and disinfect the surface, then replace the barrier
Leave the barrier off for the next patient

candidates.explanation: A contaminated underlying surface needs cleaning and disinfection before a fresh barrier. Covering contamination, dry wiping alone, or omitting the barrier does not complete decontamination.

candidates.questionText: An unbarriered clinical contact surface has visible blood. After cleaning, which disinfectant category does CDC recommend?

answers.text: An FDA-cleared high-level instrument disinfectant
An EPA-registered low-level hospital disinfectant
A detergent without a hospital-disinfectant claim
An EPA-registered tuberculocidal hospital disinfectant

candidates.explanation: Visible blood calls for the specified intermediate-level product, used as labeled. Low-level disinfection or detergent alone is insufficient; high-level instrument chemicals should not be used on environmental surfaces.

candidates.questionText: A reusable receptor holder contacts oral mucosa and its validated instructions permit heat sterilization. What processing is appropriate between patients?

answers.text: Clean and heat-sterilize it according to its instructions
Rinse it and fit a new barrier only
Use surface disinfectant instead of sterilization
Store it until visible contamination dries

candidates.explanation: This heat-tolerant semicritical item requires heat sterilization after cleaning. Rinsing/barriers, surface disinfection alone, and drying are not substitutes. This does not prescribe processing for electronic sensors.

candidates.questionText: A packaged, sterilized heat-tolerant receptor holder is found in a torn pouch before use. What should the assistant do?

answers.text: Use it if the original date is recent
Reprocess it with cleaning, packaging and heat sterilization
Tape the tear and use it
Move it to a new pouch without reprocessing

candidates.explanation: A torn package compromises maintained sterility. CDC calls for complete reprocessing; a recent date, tape, or a replacement pouch alone cannot restore it.

candidates.questionText: A receptor-positioning accessory is labeled single-use. What should happen after its use for one patient’s procedure?

answers.text: Clean it for the next patient
Keep it until it looks worn
Dispose of it appropriately
Sterilize it to convert it into a reusable item

candidates.explanation: Single-use devices are not intended for routine reprocessing and reuse by the dental office. Cleaning, keeping, or sterilizing the accessory does not change its intended use.

candidates.questionText: When does hand hygiene belong in the sequence for wearing examination gloves?

answers.text: Only at the start of the workday
Only if a tear is visible
Only after all patients have been seen
Immediately before putting them on and after removing them

candidates.explanation: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Small defects and removal can contaminate hands, so waiting for visible damage or a workday boundary is inadequate.

candidates.questionText: After glove removal, an assistant’s hands are visibly soiled. Which hand-hygiene method should be used?

answers.text: Wash with soap and water
Apply alcohol hand rub without washing
Cover the soil with clean gloves
Wipe the hands on a dry towel

candidates.explanation: CDC specifies soap and water for visibly soiled hands. Alcohol rub alone, covering with gloves, and dry wiping do not meet that recommendation.

candidates.questionText: A chemical indicator changed color in a sterilized instrument package. How should that finding be used?

answers.text: As permission to stop biological monitoring
Alongside mechanical and biological monitoring
As a replacement for reviewing cycle parameters
As proof that cleaning before sterilization was unnecessary

candidates.explanation: Chemical indicators are one part of monitoring, not a substitute for mechanical or biological checks. A color change also does not remove the need for cleaning.
